item.title: City withdraws motion to dismiss Open Meetings Act lawsuit over city manager hiring, will answer by Aug. 14
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo City Commission has withdrawn its motion to dismiss a lawsuit accusing it of violating the state's Open Meetings Act during the process that led to the hiring of City Manager Robert Stockwell, according to a notice filed in the Twelfth Judicial District Court.

The notice, filed July 31 by the city's outside counsel, Dixon•Scholl•Carrillo P.A., withdraws the Commission's Motion to Dismiss or in the Alternative Motion for More Definite Statement "in its entirety" and states the city will file a formal Answer to the underlying petition by Friday, Aug. 14.

The case, Chris Edwards v. The Alamogordo City Commission, No. D-1215-CV-2026-00514, was filed June 2 in Otero County district court and assigned to Judge Lori L. Gibson Willard. The petition alleges the Commission violated the Open Meetings Act, NMSA 1978, §§ 10-15-1 to -4, and the Inspection of Public Records Act, NMSA 1978, §§ 14-2-1 to -12, in connection with a series of closed executive sessions concerning the city manager position between March and June of this year.

According to the petition, the Commission voted unanimously, 7-0, on March 10 to direct staff to negotiate a city manager contract with then-Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez. Weeks of closed executive sessions followed. On April 28, within minutes of reconvening from one such session, the Commission voted 4-3 to accept a separation settlement with Hernandez rather than finalize her contract — without public debate nor terms disclosure, the petition alleges a failure to disclose any settlement terms or explaining the reversal in open session.

The city manager position was ultimately filled on June 15, when the Commission voted 5-2 to hire Robert Stockwell following another closed session. The petition contends the actual selection process took place behind closed doors and that the public votes served only to ratify decisions already made in private.

The city has disputed that characterization. In its now-withdrawn motion to dismiss the Commission argued that its charter authority to appoint a city manager permitted it to discuss hiring, departure negotiations, and related settlement matters in closed session under the Open Meetings Act's "limited personnel matters" and "pending litigation" exceptions, and that nothing in the statute required the Commission to disclose candidate names, contract terms, or its reasoning as a part of a public vote.

A motion to dismiss, if granted, can end some or all of a lawsuit's claims before the case proceeds further. By withdrawing its motion, the Commission avoids a ruling on whether the petition's allegations were legally sufficient to proceed — but it also leaves those allegations unresolved, rather than adjudicated in the city's favor.

The withdrawal came 10 days after the court entered a stipulated order granting the city leave to file a sur-reply — a further round of briefing — in support of its motions related to an IPRA. Instead, it withdrew the motion outright for dismissal and the case will now proceed.

The case had been set for a hearing on the motion Aug. 12, 2026. With no motion left pending, Edwards is filing a notice asking the court to vacate that August 12th hearing as moot, or to clarify its purpose if the court intends to use the time for another matter.

Under the city's own notice, an Answer to the petition — the city's formal, paragraph-by-paragraph response admitting or denying each allegation — is due Aug. 14. 

That filing will mark the first point in the case where the city responds to the specific factual allegations in the petition rather than arguing for dismissal on legal grounds.

Separately, a motion asking the court to compel the city's compliance with a pending public-records request — covering city manager candidate scoring materials and other records — has been fully briefed since early July and remains awaiting a ruling.

Alamogordo Town News will continue to report on developments in the case as they occur.

This article is based on filings of public record in the Twelfth Judicial District Court, Otero County. Copies of the referenced filings are available through the Otero County Clerk's office.

item.title: Holloman's Big Give Closes with Celebration at Casa Motors: 19 Teams, Thousands of Volunteer Hours, and a Community That Won Big
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The 2026 Cosa Motos Holloman AFB Big Give Partnership came to a festive close Monday evening as the general manager of Casa Motors hosted a reception honoring the 19 squadron teams from Holloman Air Force Base that fanned out across Alamogordo, Tularosa and Ruidoso over the past month, contributing thousands of volunteer hours to small businesses, nonprofits and community projects across the region.

The Big Give is a month-long initiative in which Holloman squadrons partner with local communities across the Tularosa Basin and beyond to restore and improve public and commercial spaces — service beyond the mission that base officials say strengthens the bond between airmen and the communities they call home. This year's 19 projects ranged from work at the VFW Post 7686 and support for Alamogordo MainStreet to cemetery restoration and water cleanup efforts.

Monday's reception served double duty: the public cast ballots for the People's Choice honors while a voting panel weighed the field to crown the overall champions of an event in which, by every account in the room, the real winner was the community itself.

From Prime Time to the Tularosa Basin: How the Big Give Began

The Big Give tradition at Holloman traces its inspiration to an unlikely source: network television. In 2008, ABC aired “Oprah's Big Give,” a reality series created and produced by Oprah Winfrey through Harpo Productions and hosted by Nate Berkus, in which ten contestants crisscrossed the country competing not to get, but to give — taking on charitable challenges in a different city each week before a panel awarded the final $1 million prize. The show lasted only a single season, but Winfrey's parting challenge outlived it. She urged viewers not to wait for a television crew: rally your friends, your family and your neighbors, she said, and pull off your own Big Give in your own community.

Casa Motors participating with Team Holloman took her up on it. In the years that followed, base leadership and community partners organized the first Casa Motors Big Give, adapting the show's format into a friendly squadron-versus-squadron competition with a distinctly local purpose — pouring airmen's sweat equity into the small businesses, nonprofits and public spaces of Otero County. What began as a television-inspired experiment has grown into one of the most anticipated annual traditions in the base-community relationship: a full month in which squadrons scout projects, adopt organizations in need of a volunteer boost, and compete for bragging rights measured not in dollars raised but in fences painted, exhibits rebuilt, murals completed and hours given.

Nearly two decades on, the format remains true to its origins — teams, projects, judges and awards — but the stakes have inverted from the television version. On the show, one contestant walked away with a million dollars. At Holloman, the prize pool is the community itself, and this year it paid out across three towns: from a fresh mural and refurbished overhang on New York Avenue completed by the 54th Operations Support Squadron in Alamogordo's historic downtown, to cemetery restorations, water cleanups and the transformation of the zoo's bird exhibit.

2026 Big Give Honors

Award

Recipient

Community Choice Award

29th Attack Squadron

Small Team Award

314th Fighter Squadron

Large Team Award

49th Equipment Maintenance Squadron — Alameda Park Zoo bird exhibit

The Large Team Award recognized the 49th Equipment Maintenance Squadron for its major renovation work at the bird exhibit at the Alameda Park Zoo — one of the most ambitious undertakings in this year's slate of projects.

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald told the gathering she was "deeply moved by the level of effort Holloman personnel brought to the community this year, taking on 19 projects that touched everything from the VFW post and Alamogordo MainStreet to local cemeteries and regional water cleanup initiatives."


“The Big Give exemplifies Holloman’s commitment to community, family and mission.”

— Col. Michael S. Mullin, 49th Wing commander

Col. Michael S. Mullin, who assumed command of the 49th Wing on June 4, said he was proud of his airmen's effort and looks forward "to even deeper engagement with the broader Alamogordo and Otero County community." Mullin said the Casa Motors Big Give exemplifies Holloman's mission pillars of community, family and mission — and added that he and his family "love being back in Alamogordo for his second tour at the base."

Mullin knows at least one of this year's winning teams well: he served as director of operations and then commander of the 314th Fighter Squadron — this year's Small Team Award winner — during his first Holloman assignment from 2018 to 2021, before returning this summer from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, where he was deputy commander of the 354th Fighter Wing.

With thousands  airmen, family members and civilian employees, Holloman's population accounts for more than a third of the Alamogordo area — and events like the Casa Motors Big Give are a visible reminder that the relationship runs in both directions. 

Alamogordo and Holloman were jointly recognized with the Altus Trophy, the Air Force community-support honor, underscoring a partnership both the city and the base continue to invest in.

As the applause faded Monday night and the award winners found their new homes, the scoreboard was clear: 19 teams, three awards, thousands of hours — and one community better for all of it.

item.title: Recent Suicide and Escape Highlight Ongoing Issues at For-Profit Facility Of Lincoln County Jail
item.description:
An inmate who escaped from the Lincoln County Jail has been apprehended, law enforcement officials confirmed. The recapture ended a search that heightened concerns about security at the facility, which is already facing scrutiny over chronic understaffing and inadequate oversight.

Escape and Recapture

Ralph Miranda escaped from the Lincoln County Detention Center but was taken into custody by Lincoln County Sheriff’s Deputies in Carrizozo a short time after his escape.

The rapid apprehension involved a coordinated multi-agency response, according to Sheriff Michael Wood. The following agencies assisted in the capture:

• Carrizozo Police Department

• New Mexico State Police

• Capitan Police Department

• Ruidoso Police Department

Sheriff Wood released a statement thanking all responding agencies for their quick action and coordinated efforts, which resulted in Miranda’s swift recapture and helped ensure community safety.

Two Crises in Days Raise Critical Questions

The escape occurs just days after an inmate died by suicide at the Lincoln County Detention Center—a death that occurred in a cell equipped with video monitoring. The incident has prompted urgent questions about supervision protocols, staff availability, and whether appropriate intervention measures were in place.

The back-to-back crises—the suicide followed by the escape—have intensified community and official scrutiny of operational safety at the facility. Together, these incidents paint a picture of a detention center struggling under operational strain.

“The timing of these two serious incidents is alarming,” said observers monitoring the situation. “When you have a suicide followed by an escape within days, it raises fundamental questions about whether this facility is being properly managed and staffed.”

Broader Context: Systemic Staffing Crisis

The escape incident comes as the Lincoln County Detention Center, operated by private corrections company CSG (Corrections Services Group), faces a critical contract renewal decision scheduled for October. Sheriff Wood has indicated that a full investigation into the escape will be underway and one is ongoing into the suicide per sources within the Department as well. 

However, the escape occurs against a backdrop of more profound operational concerns that have mounted over recent weeks:

Chronic Understaffing and Excessive Overtime: The detention center has been operating significantly understaffed, with correctional officers regularly working excessive overtime shifts. This chronic staffing shortage has persisted despite corrections experts questioning whether current staff levels meet optimal requirements for a facility of this size and inmate population.

Dangerous Medical Support Gaps: Perhaps most critically, there is no nurse or medical personnel stationed at the facility during overnight shifts. This absence of immediate medical response capability raises serious questions about the facility’s ability to respond to inmate medical emergencies—a concern made more acute by last week’s inmate suicide, which occurred in a monitored cell.

Staff Fatigue and Supervision Concerns: 

The excessive overtime required by understaffing has raised concerns among both staff and outside observers about whether tired, overworked officers can maintain adequate supervision and respond appropriately to crises. When a facility is continuously short-handed, the quality of oversight deteriorates.

Suppression of Incident Reporting: Sources with the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Department have alleged that jail leadership has discouraged staff from reporting operational problems and safety concerns to the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, potentially limiting critical oversight by elected officials responsible for the facility. This alleged suppression of reporting raises questions about accountability and transparency.

Public Records Request Seeks Accountability: 

Alamogordo Town News has filed an Information and Public Records Act (IPRA) request seeking documentation on:

• Staffing levels at the time of the recent suicide

• Optimal staffing levels for the facility

• Current inmate census

• Documentation of the suicide incident and staffing conditions

• Issues surrounding the pending contract renewal

October Contract Renewal Becomes Critical

The October contract renewal with CSG now takes on heightened significance. Lincoln County officials—including the Sheriff’s Office and County Commission—will face pressure to address fundamental questions:

• Can CSG adequately manage this facility with current staffing levels?

• What assurances will the company provide regarding medical staffing for overnight shifts?

• How will the county ensure that incident reporting is not suppressed?

• What oversight mechanisms will be put in place to prevent future incidents?

• Should the county consider alternative operators or increased public management?

The renewal decision will effectively signal whether Lincoln County is committed to addressing these critical safety and operational issues or willing to continue under the status quo.

Next Steps

Alamogordo Town News’s IPRA request for incident documentation and staffing records will provide crucial information about whether claims of understaffing and inadequate oversight are borne out by official records. The responses to this public records request will likely shape the contract renewal discussion in October.

item.title: In Memory of Laura Ann Peek
item.description:
Laura Ann Peek passed away at the hospital in El Paso, TX on July 25, 2026. She was born on September 26, 1964, to Thomas L. and Lynne E. Peek in Key West, Florida. She was the oldest daughter of 4 children.

Being a Navy family for 20 years, Laura traveled a lot with us. First home for her was Key West and then on to San Diego, CA for a number of years. After that, on to North Gower, Ontario, Canada for our last duty station. During these travels, we went through lots of places, Washington DC, Texas, Tennessee, Missouri, New York, New Hampshire, and Vermont.

After retiring from military life, we settled for a while on 16 Springs Rd.in NM. Like in Canada, we raised sheep, 2 calves and a garden, which she helped with. We had lots of dogs as pets. We lived in Cloudcroft, NM a short while where Laura finished school at Cloudcroft High School. From there we moved down the mountain to Alamogordo, NM.

Laura was with us till the age of 36. She then moved to a small group home in Las Cruces, NM for 24-hour care. She enjoyed getting out into the community and travel with caregivers to Disneyland, CA, Albuquerque Zoo and museums, and Ruidoso, NM.

Her father Thomas, passed away in 2018. Laura is survived by her sisters, Susan Schexnayder of Arvada, CO and Michelle Collins and husband Dusty of Alamogordo; her brother, Steven Peek of Alamogordo; nephew, Dustin Schexnayder of Wheat Ridge, CO; niece, Casen Collins Fisher and husband Austin of Fitchburg, WI.

Even with Laura's disabilities, she had a full life and many happy memories.

Burial will be held at Monte Vista Cemetery at a later date.

In lieu of flowers, please donate to the Epilepsy Foundation or a charity of your choice.

item.title: Crisis at Lincoln County Correctional Center: A Troubling Pattern Emerges as Private Operator Seeks Contract Renewal
item.description:
A cascade of serious incidents at Lincoln County Detention Center has reignited debate over whether for-profit corporations should be running county jail facilities, raising pressing questions about accountability, oversight, and public safety.

The troubled facility has been beset by a pattern of concerning incidents in recent weeks: a suicide, reports of severe understaffing, an inmate escape, and most damaging of all, allegations of gross misconduct by a compliance officer whose explicit duty was to ensure the jail followed state and federal law.

Yet despite these crises, the for-profit operator running the facility is seeking renewal of its contract with Lincoln County—a development that has sparked outrage among those questioning whether private corrections corporations should hold county jail contracts at all.

A Compliance Officer's Breach of Trust

The most egregious case involves Leticia Amaya, 35, the jail's compliance manager—the very person tasked with ensuring the facility adhered to state and federal regulations, including the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA).

Instead, Amaya allegedly conducted a sexual relationship with an inmate in her custody, becoming pregnant with his child and engaging in sexual encounters in a mop closet and other areas of the jail facility.

Amaya now faces three counts of criminal sexual penetration and one count of tampering with evidence. According to court documents filed in 12th Judicial District Court, the relationship with the inmate occurred roughly between July and September 2025.

While the court records indicate the relationship appeared consensual, PREA explicitly prohibits prison or jail officials from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with inmates—a prohibition Amaya, as compliance manager, was specifically hired to enforce. The very person responsible for holding the jail accountable to federal law became the subject of federal law violations.

Damning Details Emerge

Investigation by the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office revealed the extent of the breach in court records. When the began investigating after learning of the relationship, leaders listened to recorded jail phone calls between Amaya and the inmate.

"It was obvious that the two were in a relationship, as they used terms of endearment," staff leadership told detectives, according to a criminal complaint filed by Detective Bryce Bailey.

The inmate had been held at the facility between May 2025 and September 2025. According to documents, Amaya and the inmate had sexual encounters multiple times, including in a mop closet, a booking area closet, and a vacant cell he was painting.

When confronted with recordings of jail phone calls in which she told the inmate she was pregnant, Amaya initially denied the relationship and falsely claimed the baby belonged to her ex-husband. She eventually admitted the truth: she was pregnant with the inmate's child, had engaged in a "boyfriend and girlfriend" relationship with him while he was incarcerated, and had violated the very federal law she was hired to protect.

Amaya was charged in February 2025 and is currently free on her own recognizance. A trial is scheduled for December.

Broader Pattern of Failure

The Amaya case is not an isolated incident, but rather the most visible manifestation of a troubling pattern at LCDC.

In recent weeks, the facility has experienced:

A suicide that has raised questions about mental health protocols and staffing levels with pending IPRA requests seeking information and details. 

Critical short-staffing that has compromised security and operations

An inmate escape that exposed vulnerabilities in facility management and security procedures

These incidents collectively paint a picture of a facility spinning out of control, with inadequate supervision, insufficient staffing, and a breakdown in the chain of command and institutional accountability.

The Private Prison Debate: Why Should Corporations Run County Jails?

The ongoing crisis at LCDC has renewed a fundamental question: Why are for-profit corporations running county jail facilities instead of locally accountable sheriff's departments?

Unlike public jails operated directly by sheriff's departments, private jail operators have a financial incentive to minimize costs—often at the expense of staffing, training, and oversight. They are accountable to distant corporate headquarters and shareholders, not to the communities they serve.

A county sheriff, by contrast, is directly elected and answers to county voters. A sheriff oversees the jail as part of a broader law enforcement mission, with institutional stability and community accountability built into the governance structure.

"There's an inherent conflict of interest when a corporation profits from incarceration," critics argue. "Cost-cutting directly impacts safety, and when something goes wrong, the corporation can simply decline to renew a contract and move on, leaving the community to pick up the pieces."

Contract Renewal Under a Cloud

Against this backdrop, the private operator's bid for a new contract in Lincoln County raises troubling questions. How can the county justify renewing a contract with a corporation that:

Has lost operational control of the facility, as evidenced by a suicide, an escape, and staffing crises?

Employed a compliance manager who violated the very federal law she was hired to enforce?

Has documented problems with institutional oversight and accountability?

Prioritizes profit margins over adequate staffing and security?

County officials face a critical decision point and citizens must demand answers. Do they continue with a failing private model, or do they consider bringing jail operations back under public control, where accountability runs through elected sheriff leadership rather than corporate management structures?

Questions Without Answers

As Amaya awaits trial, and as LCDC continues to grapple with the fallout from multiple crises, the underlying questions remain unanswered:

Where was the management oversight that should have caught Amaya's relationship before it progressed to pregnancy?

Why was understaffing allowed to reach levels that contributed to a suicide and an escape?

What institutional failures permitted a compliance officer to violate the very federal statutes she was responsible for upholding?

And most fundamentally: Should Lincoln County continue entrusting its jail to a for-profit corporation, or should it demand that a public agency—accountable to voters—manage the facility?

These are not academic questions. They go to the heart of public safety, institutional accountability, and the basic principle that those who deprive people of their liberty must be subject to rigorous public oversight.

As Lincoln County considers the private operator's contract renewal request, the answer to these questions will determine whether the facility can rebuild public trust or whether it continues on its current troubling trajectory.

item.title: Court of Appeals Denies Republican Party’s Final Appeal in Barela Leadership Dispute
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — In what may be the final chapter of a bitter intra-party legal battle, New Mexico’s Court of Appeals has denied the Republican Party of New Mexico’s petition for writ of error on August 5, 2026, effectively upholding the lower court’s controversial decision to remove Amy Barela from her position as state party chairwoman.

The three-judge appellate panel, consisting of Justices Jacqueline R. Medina, J. Miles Hanisee, and Gerald E. Baca, remanded the matter back to Otero County District Court for further proceedings. The order closes a legal chapter that has roiled the state’s Republican Party for months and raised questions about the judiciary’s proper role in resolving internal party disputes.

A Party at War with Itself

The conflict that led to this ruling originated when two separate lawsuits were filed in May 2026 seeking the ouster of state GOP chairwoman Amy Barela, with one filed in Bernalillo County and another in Otero County. The plaintiffs — including lieutenant governor candidate Aubrey Blair Dunn, Otero County Commission candidate Jonathan Emery, gubernatorial candidate Duke Rodriguez, and other party members — argued that Barela had violated party rules by refusing to step aside while simultaneously seeking re-election to her Otero County Commission seat.

The central issue hinged on the Republican Party’s own internal rules. Party rules prohibit chairpersons from holding the post while also running in a contested primary. This conflict-of-interest provision was designed to prevent party leaders from using their official positions to advantage their own candidacies.

The Lower Court’s Dramatic Ruling

On May 27, 2026, Thirteenth Judicial District Judge Cindy Mercer issued a preliminary injunction that prohibits Barela from continuing to serve as chair and also orders party officials not to publicly support any of the Republicans running for office during the ongoing primary.

The injunction came just days before the June 2 primary election and sent shockwaves through Republican circles. Aubrey Blair Dunn, who is running for lieutenant governor as a Republican and was one of the plaintiffs, said the party’s decision to appeal is misguided, stating “The judge’s decision was clear, well-reasoned, and plainly correct, and dragging it into an appeal does nothing but waste the Party’s limited resources and the Court’s valuable time.” Gubernatorial candidate Duke Rodriguez, another plaintiff, said an appeal will only distract from the Republican Party’s efforts to win elections.

The Party’s Appeal and Supreme Court Loss

Undeterred by these comments from fellow Republicans, the party and Barela herself filed an emergency petition to the New Mexico Supreme Court. The Republican Party of New Mexico argued that a lower court judge’s ruling was unprecedented and “extraordinary”.

The New Mexico Supreme Court on June 10, 2026, denied the Republican Party of New Mexico’s appeal of the lower court ruling. The state Republican party filed an emergency petition on May 29, arguing it violated party members’ free speech rights and that courts are not the proper venue to resolve intra-party disputes. The New Mexico Supreme Court unanimously denied that petition without explanation.

That rebuke at the state’s highest court set the stage for today’s appellate court decision, which further demonstrates the judicial system’s determination to enforce the will of the lower court.

Political Consequences and Timing

The legal battle’s impact on the 2026 election cycle was immediate and profound. Amy Barela was ousted from the Otero County Commission by a 46-vote margin in the primary election, just days after a judge ordered her to step down from her party post.

The tight loss raises questions about whether Barela’s legal troubles affected her electoral prospects, or whether she was simply defeated by a well-organized opponent. Jonathan Emery narrowly beat Barela in the June 2 primary election.

A Fractious Party

The dispute reflects deeper divisions within New Mexico’s Republican Party heading into a critical election year. The party has struggled with leadership and message coherence, particularly on statewide races. The internal legal war has consumed resources and attention that many Republicans believe should have been focused on challenging Democratic control of state offices.

The broader context involves questions about presidential loyalties within the state GOP. Though not explicitly stated in court documents, the lawsuit emerged amid broader national Republican tensions between traditional party conservatives and more populist wings.

What Happens Next

With the Court of Appeals having remanded the case back to District Court, the matter is not entirely resolved. The lower court will likely address remaining questions about party governance and potential damages. Additionally, questions remain about how the party will move forward in selecting new leadership.

Earlier this summer, the party was scheduled to name a new chair at a June 20 State Central Committee meeting in Las Cruces, though the full details of that process and whether all leadership questions have been resolved remain unclear.

A Lawyer’s Perspective

Aubrey Blair Dunn, one of the plaintiffs and himself a lawyer serving Albuquerque in Administrative Law and Appeals cases, viewed the case as a straightforward application of existing party rules. The Court of Appeals’ decision appears to validate his interpretation that judges do have a role to play when internal party matters rise to the level of contractual disputes governed by written bylaws and rules.

The ruling also suggests that while courts generally try to avoid interfering in internal party politics, they will intervene when a party’s own written rules have been clearly violated and members take legal action.

Looking Forward

Today’s decision by the Court of Appeals effectively closes one chapter of the Republican Party’s internal warfare, though questions remain about whether this ruling will be the final word or if further legal challenges are possible.

For Barela, the defeat marks a dramatic fall from power for the chairwoman who led the party into 2026. She remains an Otero County resident and her political future remains uncertain.

For the plaintiffs — including Dunn, Emery, and Rodriguez — the wins in court and at the ballot box represent vindication of their position that party rules exist to prevent exactly the kind of conflict-of-interest situation Barela allegedly created.

For the New Mexico Republican Party itself, the question now becomes whether it can move forward unified under new leadership, or whether the bitterness of this legal fight will continue to hamper Republican efforts to regain statewide offices.
